papers.title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: This paper compares different computational methods for segmenting cells in spatial transcriptomics data, where identifying accurate cell boundaries is a major technical challenge. It likely evaluates accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency across various segmentation algorithms using benchmark datasets. The goal is to guide researchers in choosing the most reliable segmentation approach for their spatial data analysis pipelines.
papers.why: Accurate cell segmentation is a critical first step for any spatial transcriptomics analysis of neurons and interneurons, directly impacting the reliability of downstream findings on mitophagy and perineuronal net-related gene expression in brain tissue.

papers.title: Donor-Cell Senescence Redirects PINK1-Marked Mitochondrial Cargo From Mitophagy to Microvesicle Transfer Through SUMO3-Stabilized HSPA9.
papers.summary: This paper studies how senescent (aging) cells handle damaged mitochondria tagged with PINK1, a key protein marking mitochondria for mitophagy (degradation). Instead of destroying these mitochondria through normal mitophagy, senescent cells package them into microvesicles and send them to other cells, a process controlled by SUMO3 modification stabilizing the protein HSPA9. This reveals a previously unknown escape route for damaged mitochondrial cargo that bypasses degradation and instead spreads it intercellularly.
papers.why: This mechanism of PINK1-mediated mitophagy rerouting via intercellular mitochondrial transfer is relevant background for understanding alternative fates of mitochondrial quality control pathways that could inform interpretation of neuronal mitophagy dynamics, even though the paper itself does not focus on neurons or brain tissue.

papers.title: Receptor-Specific ER-Phagy in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms and Emerging Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how cells selectively degrade parts of the endoplasmic reticulum through a process called ER-phagy, focusing on specific receptor proteins that tag ER fragments for autophagic clearance. It explains how dysfunction in these receptor-specific pathways contributes to the buildup of misfolded proteins and cellular stress seen in neurodegenerative diseases. The review also discusses potential therapeutic strategies that could target these ER-phagy receptors to restore proper cellular clearance mechanisms in neurons.
papers.why: Although focused on ER-phagy rather than mitophagy specifically, this paper is relevant because it covers selective autophagy pathways in neurons that may intersect mechanistically with mitophagy regulation in neurodegeneration.
papers.figure: A schematic figure illustrating the molecular pathways of different ER-phagy receptors and their roles in neuronal protein quality control.

papers.title: Ferritinophagy ignites GSDMD activation: selective autophagy links iron metabolism to innate immunity.
papers.summary: This paper reports that ferritinophagy, a selective form of autophagy that degrades the iron-storage protein ferritin, triggers activation of GSDMD, a protein that forms membrane pores during inflammatory cell death. The study shows a direct molecular link between how cells manage iron and how they trigger innate immune responses. This connects autophagy machinery to inflammation in a new way, beyond its classic role in clearing damaged organelles like mitochondria.
papers.why: Although focused on iron and immunity rather than neurons, this work expands understanding of selective autophagy pathways that could inform how mitophagy and related organelle-clearance mechanisms intersect with inflammatory signaling in brain tissue.

papers.title: Engineered SHED-EVs delivering FtMt siRNA rescue mitophagy and bone formation in smoking-related osteoporosis.
papers.summary: This study engineers small extracellular vesicles (EVs) from stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED) to deliver siRNA targeting FtMt (mitochondrial ferritin). The treatment restores proper mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria) and improves bone formation in a model of smoking-related osteoporosis. The work suggests a cell-free, engineered-EV approach could reverse bone loss caused by smoking-induced mitochondrial dysfunction.
papers.why: Although this paper is about bone rather than brain, it offers a transferable engineered-EV/siRNA strategy for correcting mitophagy dysfunction that could inspire analogous delivery approaches for modulating mitophagy in neurons.

papers.title: Arsenic promotes MIN6 cells dysfunction via ACO2-αKG-mitophagy pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates how arsenic exposure damages MIN6 cells, a type of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cell line. The researchers found that arsenic disrupts the enzyme ACO2, which alters alpha-ketoglutarate (αKG) levels, ultimately triggering abnormal mitophagy (the selective degradation of damaged mitochondria). This pathway leads to beta cell dysfunction, suggesting a mechanism by which arsenic exposure could contribute to diabetes-related cell damage.
papers.why: Although this paper focuses on pancreatic beta cells rather than neurons, it provides mechanistic insight into the ACO2-αKG-mitophagy pathway that could inform understanding of similar mitochondrial quality control mechanisms potentially relevant to neuronal mitophagy research.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed ACO2-αKG-mitophagy signaling pathway diagram, illustrating how arsenic exposure connects to mitochondrial dysfunction and autophagy induction.

papers.title: PINK1-mediated mitophagy supports lung cancer initiation and limits the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapy
papers.summary: This paper investigates how PINK1-mediated mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria, helps lung cancer cells survive and initiate tumors. The researchers found that this mitophagy pathway also reduces the effectiveness of drugs targeting KRAS mutations, a common cancer driver. By studying PINK1 in this cancer context, the authors suggest that blocking mitophagy could improve KRAS-targeted cancer treatments.
papers.why: Although focused on lung cancer rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into PINK1-mediated mitophagy pathways that are directly relevant to understanding mitochondrial quality control processes being studied in neuronal contexts.

papers.title: APPL1 attenuates DHEA-induced oxidative injury in granulosa cells by enhancing mitophagy and suppressing ferroptosis: implications for polycystic ovary syndrome.
papers.summary: This study looks at granulosa cells (ovarian cells) that have been damaged by excess DHEA, a hormone linked to polycystic ovary syndrome. The researchers found that a protein called APPL1 helps protect these cells by boosting mitophagy, the process of clearing out damaged mitochondria, and by blocking ferroptosis, a form of iron-dependent cell death. Overall, APPL1 appears to reduce oxidative stress and cell damage in this PCOS model.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on ovarian cells rather than neurons, its mechanistic insights into mitophagy regulation and its protective role against oxidative stress and ferroptosis could inform parallel investigations of mitophagy pathways in neurons and interneurons within the brain.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin, LC3) and ferroptosis indicators (e.g., lipid peroxidation, GPX4 levels) in APPL1-overexpressing versus control granulosa cells treated with DHEA.
